Q: How to "sync" Prisma with sessions? A:

You can technically let connect-pg-simple create the table for you, but I think it's better to create a prisma model for the sessions table and migrate to make prisma know that a session table exists, and avoid any issues later with migrations. I don't really get why you think it's ugly, but you can change the name of the properties to friendlier names and use @map to map them correctly to the column names on the db. I personally always create a model for sessions and extend it with my own properties, for features like manually revoking sessions and for example showing users their active sessions and allowing them to terminate them. It can be quite useful sometimes.

Q: How can I require a delegate/lambda to be static? A:

What you want is only partially possible with C#. Most your requirements are not. In addition, the side-effect-free/thread-safe part is probably a design smell.

Your first requirement:

I write a method that accepts a delegate as a parameter I find the need to require that the passed delegate must be static

Your current test is almost right. You just ignore the fact that created delegates are usually MultiCastDelegate, so they can combine multiple delegates. Therefore, checking Delegate.Method.IsStatic or Delegate.Target == null is not sufficient. You should instead inspect the invocation list:

// Can only test static methods and not lambdas
public static bool IsReferencingStaticMethods(System.Delegate del) => del.GetInvocationList()
    .All(d => d.Method.IsStatic);

Delegate.Target == null is not robust. Microsoft docs say:

If the delegate invokes one or more instance methods, this property returns the target of the last instance method in the invocation list.

The consequence is that Delegate.Target == null will fail for MultiCastDelegate type delegates.
Additionally, delegates can be nested.

Important: Delegate.Method.IsStatic, or the Delegate API in general, can only test for static methods and not lambdas declared with the static keyword. In other words, inspecting the Delegate instance can only assure you that the delegate is backed by an actual static method.

For lambdas, Steven Toub wrotes:

The static keyword when applied to a lambda has zero impact on the generated code. It serves only to enforce that the body of the lambda doesn't close over non-static state. Whether the emmitted method for the lambda is actually an instance or static method is an implementation detail of the C# compiler, and as you saw, your code today will result in an instance method (for performance reasons).

This means lambdas decorated with static are pure compiler features. The important nuance is that it is only a promise that the lambda itself won't capture any non-static context (like locals or instance variables).
It does not give any guarantees how the emitted code for that lambda looks like. It can be a static or an instance method, depending on how the compiler decides to optimize.
But the optimization decision making is independent from the static keyword.

The important part is: static applied to lambdas has a totally different meaning than static has when applied to members.
Much like C# reuses the same keyword readonly for different features. The compiler decides based on the context what the keyword means.

According to this information, what you can do is to write a Roslyn analyzer that checks whether the lambda captures any context. If it doesn't capture, then still the lambda could be decorated with the static keyword or just be a normal lambda that just captures no context.
You can only validate that a lambda is not capturing any non-static context. There is no language level feature to enforce that constraint on the caller during compile time.

If knowing that the lambda did not capture any context is sufficient then this solution will work.

If you need to explicitly test whether the lambda was declared using static, then this is not possible since the compiler translates static into a context rule where the emitted method's arguments simply must not reference context outside the lambda.
Once this constraint is satisfied, the compiler emits a simple method.

Your second requirement:

To make this truly thread safe, I need to ensure that P and R are immutable

Your third requirement:

I also need to ensure that asyncDelegate is free from side-effects

Both requirements are impossible to solve with normal C# especially with the shape of your generic method.

I would also argue that this design requirement reflects a design smell. You are asking the caller to know about the implementation details of the called API. This is just bad design. I don't know your goal so I can't suggest a better design but you should definitely review your design choices.

When a caller invokes an object it can never guarantee that the implementation is thread-safe or pure (side-effect free). Instead you must either design the API called by your method thread-safe and pure or document the requirement of your method so that callers of your method know that their arguments are required to satisfy a contract: be pure and thread-safe.
This responsibility is completely on the caller of your API. Your API can only guarantee to be itself thread-safe and pure. But it can't provide that guarantee for external API (e.g., the method arguments).

If you insist on that design, the closest you can get is a simple side-effect check using a Roslyn analyzer to inspect the internals of the arguments line by line to ensure they don't mutate any objects or members. You could look for readonly members. But after all, you will not get any guarantee unless you have analyzed the complete call tree of the external API you are to invoke. It's not possible. That's probably a reason why readonlymembers only guarantee purity for the called scope and not the full call tree.

For example, an object invokes a service or raises an event. It's impossible for you to reliably inspect the service and the listeners. Because a call to a service or a event listener can round trip and modify some contextually unrelated code. Even invoking a HTTP request can involve remote side-effects. Just to give an example how complex tracking side-effects is.

In my opinion, requirement 1 is possible with the caveat that you are happy to know whether the lambda does not capture context. But you can't enforce static lambdas. Requirements 2 and 3 are not possible and not desirable in that I would recommend to change the design instead of writing that highly complex code that will likely have issues and in the end naturally not able to give you a reliable validation.

Q: Assign the variable inside configure.ac A:

Remember always that Autoconf's primary job is to generate configure, which is a shell script. If configure doesn't behave as you expect then you always have the option to debug it directly. You will typically see a great deal of code corresponding to Autoconf macros, but your template text and the generated code around it shouldn't be too hard to find via your text editor's search feature.

When I gave it this input derived from the question ...

AC_INIT([so_test], [0.0.1])
SQLANY=\`set | grep "SQLANY\[09\]\*"\`
AC_MSG_NOTICE([Variable is $SQLANY])
AC_CONFIG_FILES([Makefile])
AC_OUTPUT

Autoconf generated a configure script containing this corresponding code (plus much more):

SQLANY=\`set | grep "SQLANY\09\\*"\`
{ printf "%s\n" "$as_me:${as_lineno-$LINENO}: Variable is $SQLANY" >&5
printf "%s\n" "$as_me: Variable is $SQLANY" >&6;}
ac_config_files="$ac_config_files Makefile"

Running it produced this output:

grep: warning: stray \ before 0 configure: Variable is configure: creating ./config.status config.status: creating Makefile

, with the message from grep going to stderr and the rest to stdout. A bit more experimentation confirms what you might expect, that grep does not produce any output to stdout when its pattern parsing fails like that.

There are several things going on here, but among the most significant is that in Autoconf, paired square brackets ([]) are the quoting delimiters. The backslash (\) is not special to Autoconf / M4. Quoting in Autoconf is a more complex subject than one might expect, so I suggest you read the relevant section of the Autoconf manual.

Secondarily, there are a few issues with the actual command you are trying to use, including at least

  • You should prefer the modern(-ish) POSIX syntax for command substitution ($(command)). That applies to all your scripting and interactive commands, not just Autoconf inputs. This has several advantages, and it is no longer remotely new.

  • The regular expression SQLANY[09]* doesn't mean what you seem to think it means. In your example, it is matching only the SQLANY part of the input, not the digits. You probably want SQLANY[0-9]{1,}, which requires one or more decimal digits after the letters, and accepts digits from 0 through 9, not just the endpoints.

  • I recommend quoting with single quotes in shell code except where you have good reason to do otherwise, such as when you want variable interpolation or a literal single-quote character.

Overall, this works for me and has the form I would recommend:

[SQLANY=$(set | grep -E 'SQLANY[0-9]{1,}')]
AC_MSG_NOTICE([Variable is $SQLANY])

There are lots of possible variations on that, especially around exactly which parts of the variable assignment are m4-quoted, and the exact form of the grep command, but I like that one for clarity, good shell style, and avoiding GNU-specific features.
